newsitem.title: USA: Ukraine plant restarts cadmium, auction also due.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine plant restarts cadmium, auction also due.

text.p: Ukrzinc, the Ukrainian zinc and cadmium producer, is to restart production this year amid renewed government efforts to auction a further wad of shares in the cash-starved company, a senior official said.
Last year Ukrzinc, shuttered since 1995, sold 15 tonnes of cadmium metal from the government stockpile, Mykola Hizenko, director of Ukrcolourprom, part of the Ukraine's ministry of industry, said.

Ukrcolourprom imports and exports raw materials and is responsible for sourcing feed for Ukrzinc. Hizenko was here to give a presentation on Ukraine's cadmium industry at Metal Bulletin's Minor Metals seminar.
Back in 1995 the government launched the first round of share auctions in Ukrzinc. The state now owns 50 percent, with 12.5 percent held by employees and the balance in private hands, Hizenko said.
The Ukraine government's Committee of State Commodities intention proposes to hike private ownership to 80 percent, but no date or terms have been announced for the auction yet, Hizenko told Reuters.

Foreign investment has shunned the plant so far, and the company has been forced to secure 20,000 tonnes of zinc concentrates from the Bolislav mine in Poland on a tolling basis for this year to produce 80 to 90 tonnes of cadmium metal, and 11,000 to 12,000 tonnes of zinc.
"We will sell a small quantity of cadmium from stockpile as well this year, and about 1,000 tonnes of zinc," Hizenko said.
He was unable to say the extent of Ukraine's cadmium stockpile. The metal is a by-product of zinc production.
Ukrzinc's production capacity is 130 tonnes a year of cadmium and 40,000 tonnes a year of zinc metal.
"We want to reach this capacity in 1998-2000," Hizenko said speaking through an interpretor. Higher output would also cut unit costs.
Global cadmium production was estimated by traders here at 18,000 tonnes a year, including a "guesstimate" of output by countries former part of the Soviet Union.
The money raised to buy the zinc concentrates this year has come from zinc customers, and the cadmium will be sold to the domestic Lugansk nickel-cadmium battery plant.
Lugansk is only operating on a two-day week shift because of the lack of raw materials and cash. "Domestic demand is substantial now and the priority should be given to that," Hizenko said.
Lugansk failed to modernise its extraction facility for handling spent batteries, and has accumulated about 100 to 110 tonnes of contained cadmium in scrap.
